newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - US inflation-buster only for cautious.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - US inflation-buster only for cautious.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury is set to launch an inflation-linked bond next week but analysts said on Friday it would only be for the faint-hearted.

Although the bond is expected to fast become the market benchmark and has certainly piqued overseas interest, analysts questioned whether the risk of higher U.S. inflation is big enough to make it worthwhile.
Higher real yields can be found elsewhere like Germany, Sweden or Canada, they said.

"There is a question of the level of inflation in the U.S. Unless that's projected to go very high indeed, the advantage of holding this type of bond is limited," said Sonja Gibbs, senior market strategist at Nomura International in London.

The Treasury will hold its first sale of index-linked debt next week, a hefty $7.0 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday. It will join Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand in offering bonds with a fixed return above the rate of inflation.
The bond has been trading in the when-issued market with a yield of around 3.5 percent and analysts expect the new bond to be priced to yield close to that.
That would put it only slightly above the real yield of 10-year cash notes, currently around 3.3 percent, assuming consumer prices at 1996's rate of 3.3 percent.
It would yield slightly less than comparable index-linked 10-year gilts with yields around 3.55 percent and below Canada's 2021 index-linked bond, currently yielding 4.19 percent.
Analysts in London agreed that the issue would be big enough to make the market respectable, although it may suffer some liquidity problems to begin with.

"This is $7.0 billion worth and that means the issue is quite sizable, so I think it will be quite good," said Nigel Richardson, bond economist at Yamaichi International in London. "This will be bought by investors, largely investment funds."
Analysts said the Treasury plans to eventually allow the coupon to be stripped off the bond which will draw in other investors, like strip funds, and bump up liquidity.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said the U.S. issue will add credibility to other index-linked markets, providing an easy reference point for gauging global real yields.

"It's something that's been lacking for some time in the global market," he said. "It's an indication of what the global real yield is, and allows us to start speculating about whether other markets are fairly valued."

Such speculation would bring the U.S. index-linked bond up short said Gibbs, pointing out Swedish 10-year bonds are likely to have a real yield of around 3.85 percent this year, Canadian bonds 4.20 percent and British bonds 3.60 percent.
Even German bonds with their historically low nominal yields, currently give a yield of 4.4 percent if mimimal inflation of 1.4 percent is taken into account, analysts said.

If U.S. inflation drops, returns on the new U.S. bond would fall accordingly, Gibbs said. Concerns about how the U.S. consumer price index is calculated are another negative, with a recent government-appointed commission estimating the cost of living is overstated by 1.1 percentage points.
"You need more to compensate you for the risk that inflation may be lower," Gibbs said.
There is of course the risk that inflation may be higher in 1997 but so far it remains remarkably restrained, analysts said.
For individuals and mutual funds looking for a safe investment however, the bond looks like a good bet.

"I certainly feel that given the rise in inflation concerns in the U.S and the downward moves we've seen in the Treasury market, it makes sense to shift some of your dollar exposure into an inflation protected product," said Edmonds at IBJ.
